checkpoints: A pessimistic row lock acquired via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (or `lock: { mode: "pessimistic_write" }`) is held for the entire duration of the transaction, so any slow work placed after the lock is acquired — an external pricing API call, a remote audit-log write, extra SELECTs — is not paid once but is paid by every concurrent writer queued behind that same SKU row.

On a hot SKU during a flash-sale spike this turns into a serialization bottleneck: ten writers stacked behind one slow transaction means the tenth waiter's latency is roughly ten times the critical section's duration, which is exactly what pushes lock waits into statement or transaction timeouts.

The critical section should be shrunk to only the operations that actually need the row lock to stay correct: acquire the lock, check `stock >= quantity`, subtract the quantity, insert the ledger row, and commit — nothing else belongs between lock acquisition and commit.

The pricing API call never reads or writes the `inv` row it is locking, so it has no correctness dependency on the transaction and can be moved to run before the transaction opens (or dropped entirely if the result isn't actually used to decide anything).

The audit-log write is a call to a third-party service with no transactional relationship to the inventory row, so it should fire after commit rather than before — this way a slow or flaky audit service can never extend how long the row lock is held.

The extra `OrderEntity` and `PromoEntity` SELECTs are read-only lookups unrelated to the decrement decision, so they should either be computed outside the transaction or removed if they were never load-bearing for the write.

Even after trimming the transaction to its minimum, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` still serializes all writers on a single row, which is adequate at moderate volume but is the wrong mechanism to absorb the peak concurrency of a flash-sale spike itself.

Offloading the hot path to an atomic in-memory counter (a Lua script doing GET, compare, and DECRBY in one EVAL) removes the database from the critical path during the burst, and the counter can be reconciled back to the durable, lock-protected `inventories` row asynchronously via a queued job or scheduled sync, with a statement/lock timeout on the DB path kept as a backstop.

The fix should be validated by measuring p99 latency and the lock-wait/timeout rate under a concurrent burst on a single SKU before and after both trimming the transaction and offloading to the atomic counter, confirming throughput rises and timeouts drop while `inventories.stock` remains correct and non-negative.

Calling `zrange(QUEUE_KEY, 0, -1)` to compute a position forces Redis to walk its entire skip list, enumerate every member, and serialize the full N-length reply before any client-side work happens - this is an O(N) operation regardless of where the target token sits in the queue.

After the full member list arrives over the wire, `indexOf(token)` performs a second O(N) linear scan on the application side, so a single position lookup pays two separate O(N) costs stacked on top of each other.

A sorted set already maintains its ordering through a skip list, so `ZRANK` can walk directly to a member's position in O(log N) and return a single integer, with no transferring or scanning of the rest of the set.

Replacing `zrange` plus `indexOf` with `zrank` eliminates both the Redis-side enumeration/serialization cost and the client-side scan cost, not just one of the two, because the entire member list never has to leave Redis in the first place.

In a waiting-room system where every visitor polls every few seconds, the true cost of an O(N) endpoint comes from concurrent polling volume, not from any expensive business logic - a million waiters each triggering a full-set fetch is what saturates Redis CPU and network bandwidth at the same time.

Checking an admitted-visitors SET with `SISMEMBER` (O(1)) before ever touching the queue lets already-admitted visitors short-circuit immediately, avoiding even an O(log N) rank lookup for requests that do not need one.

Reducing how often a million clients poll - by backing off the interval or returning a server-computed estimated wait - cuts aggregate load in a way that a faster per-call algorithm alone cannot, since it addresses the request volume rather than the per-request cost.

A complexity fix should be confirmed with a load test at realistic scale, roughly a million queue members under concurrent polling, comparing p99 latency and Redis CPU/network utilization before and after, rather than assumed correct because the new code reads cleaner.

Wrapping a read-modify-write sequence inside `dataSource.transaction` only guarantees that the transaction's own writes commit or roll back together as a unit — it says nothing about whether another transaction can read or modify the same row while the first is still in flight.

Under the default Read Committed isolation level, `manager.findOne` without a lock option is a plain snapshot read, so two concurrent transactions can each fetch the same `stock` value before either one has written its result back.

When both transactions subtract `quantity` from that same stale in-memory value and then call `manager.save`, the second write simply overwrites the first without any awareness of it — a classic lost update — so the combined amount decremented can exceed the real stock and the system oversells.

Adding `lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' }` to the `findOne` call makes TypeORM emit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on that SKU's row, which forces a second transaction's read of the same row to block until the first transaction commits or rolls back.

Once the second transaction is forced to wait, its eventual read reflects the already-decremented stock rather than a stale snapshot, which serializes every decrement against that SKU and removes the lost-update window entirely.

Atomicity (a transaction's writes committing or rolling back as one unit) and serialized access to a row (mutual exclusion between concurrent transactions touching the same data) are two separate guarantees — a transaction boundary alone provides the former but not the latter.

The locked section of code should stay as small as possible — lock, check quantity, subtract, insert the ledger row, then commit — because holding a row-level lock longer than necessary increases contention and slows down concurrent requests during a flash sale.

Firing a burst of concurrent decrement calls against a small seeded stock, such as 200 concurrent decrement-by-1 calls against a starting stock of 100, is a concrete way to validate the fix: exactly 100 calls should succeed, the remainder should fail with an insufficient-stock error, and the final stock should floor at zero without ever going negative.

A check-then-set idempotency guard that runs `redis.get` followed by a separate `redis.set` leaves a gap between the read and the write; under two concurrent requests with the same key, both calls can read `null` before either has written anything, so both pass the `if (!existing)` check and both proceed to create an order.

Splitting the guard into two round trips reopens exactly the race the idempotency key exists to close — the key was meant to make "check ownership" and "claim ownership" a single event, and turning that into two separate Redis commands recreates a window a second caller can step through, the same shape as a `SELECT` then `INSERT` race, just one layer over on Redis instead of Postgres.

Collapsing the guard into one atomic command — `SET key PENDING EX 30 NX` — fixes the race because `NX` ("set only if the key does not already exist") makes the check-and-write a single un-interruptible Redis operation, so among any number of concurrent callers exactly one `SET` returns `"OK"` and every other caller immediately gets `null`, with no gap left for two callers to both slip through.

A caller that loses the `SET NX` race should not retry the write blindly; it must issue a follow-up `GET` on the key and branch on the value — if the value is still `PENDING`, the original request is still in flight and the caller should respond with a conflict (409, retry later); if the value is a cached result, the original request already finished and the caller should return that result marked as a replay instead of creating a new order.

Even with an atomic Redis claim, the database layer still needs its own safety net: a `UNIQUE` constraint on the idempotency key column catches the case where a second write still slips past Redis, for example a `PENDING` key's TTL expiring mid-flight or a Redis flush/restart wiping the claim before the original request finished.

When the unique constraint fires, the insert throws a database error (for Postgres, a `QueryFailedError` carrying error code `23505`) rather than silently succeeding, so the calling code must catch that specific error, re-read the already-created row by the idempotency key, and return it as a replay instead of letting a raw 500 reach the client.

Correctness of the fix should be demonstrated with two concurrent requests sharing the same idempotency key: exactly one call ends up creating the order while the other is rejected or receives a replayed result, and the orders table ends up holding exactly one row for that key.

Replaying a cached idempotency result without comparing it against the incoming request body means a client that reuses the same idempotency key with a different payload — for example a changed order amount — silently receives the old, now-incorrect response instead of an error.

The correct fix for key reuse with a changed body is to store a fingerprint (a hash such as SHA-256 of the request payload) alongside the cached result at write time, then recompute and compare that fingerprint on every replay lookup: a match replays safely, a mismatch must return 422 Unprocessable Entity rather than replaying stale data or silently processing the new request as if it were unrelated.

Wrapping the Redis lock-acquisition call in a try/catch that returns an 'ACQUIRED' state on any error is a fail-open design: once Redis becomes unreachable, every concurrent request is treated as if it won the lock, so the idempotency guard stops preventing duplicates for the entire outage window rather than degrading gracefully.

Fail-closed is the correct posture for an idempotency guard: when the underlying lock store is unavailable, the operation should reject or surface a 503 Service Unavailable instead of proceeding as if the guard succeeded, because letting every request through defeats the purpose of having a guard at all.

A database UNIQUE constraint on the idempotency key is a valid last-resort safety net, but only if the application catches the resulting unique-violation error; leaving it uncaught means a legitimate concurrent retry crashes with a raw, unhandled 500 instead of receiving the successful result of the request that already completed.

Handling a caught unique-violation correctly means re-fetching the already-persisted row by its idempotency key and returning it as a replay response, mirroring the same replay behavior used on the fast Redis-cache path so that both the cache route and the database-constraint route converge on identical client-facing behavior.

Layered idempotency protection works as defense-in-depth: the cache (e.g. Redis) optimizes the common case for speed, the database unique constraint is the durable invariant that holds even when the cache is down or racing, and the body fingerprint is what distinguishes a legitimate retry of the same operation from a different operation that mistakenly reused the same key.

When reviewing a change like this, the highest-severity issues to flag first are the ones with the largest blast radius — silent data corruption from an unvalidated replay and a guard that stops guarding under failure — ahead of lower-impact concerns like unhandled exceptions surfacing as generic errors, and the review should include concrete test cases: same key with a changed body returns 422, the store being down still yields exactly one persisted record via the database constraint, and a retry racing an in-flight write replays instead of failing with a 500.
